meta.description: Yes — Frederick Douglass really said it, in his 1857 West India Emancipation speech at Canandaigua, N.Y. Verified verbatim in the printed pamphlet.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Power concedes nothing without a demand. It never did and it never will'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Frederick Douglass: his 3 August 1857 West India Emancipation address, printed that year. A rare famous-name quote that checks out verbatim.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: This is genuinely Douglass. The line comes from his “West India Emancipation” address, delivered at Canandaigua, New York, on 3 August 1857, and printed that same year in the pamphlet Two Speeches, by Frederick Douglass. The wording is confirmed verbatim in the scholarly Frederick Douglass Papers Project ↗ edition — a rare case where a famous-name quote checks out exactly.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “West India Emancipation” (the “If there is no struggle, there is no progress” address)

source.excerpt: This struggle may be a moral one, or it may be a physical one, and it may be both moral and physical, but it must be a struggle. Power concedes nothing without a demand. It never did and it never will. Find out just what any people will quietly submit to and you have found out the exact measure of injustice and wrong which will be imposed upon them, and these will continue till they are resisted with either words or blows, or with both.
trail: The scholarly Frederick Douglass Papers Project ↗ edition of the Canandaigua address carries the sentence verbatim: “Power concedes nothing without a demand. It never did and it never will.”
The line was printed in Douglass’s own lifetime in the 1857 pamphlet Two Speeches, by Frederick Douglass ↗, which prints the West India Emancipation and Dred Scott addresses together.
The speech was delivered on 3 August 1857 at Canandaigua, N.Y.; the pamphlet’s title page mis-dates it “Aug. 4th,” a printer’s slip that has propagated ever since.
source.excerptNote: The line sits inside Douglass’s most-quoted passage, which opens “If there is no struggle, there is no progress.”

author.name: Frederick Douglass
author.heading: About Frederick Douglass
author.bio: Frederick Douglass escaped slavery in Maryland in 1838 and became the nineteenth century’s most commanding Black orator, editor, and abolitionist. His autobiographies and his newspaper work made him a national voice for emancipation and equal rights. The Canandaigua “West India Emancipation” address of 1857 — source of this line and of “If there is no struggle, there is no progress” — is among the most quoted passages in American oratory.

misattribution.heading: A genuine quote — but watch the wording
misattribution.intro: For once the famous name is correct: Douglass really said this. The errors that circulate are about the wording and the date, not the author.

items.why: A common paraphrase drops the article. Douglass’s printed text reads “without a demand,” per the Papers Project edition ↗.

items.who: “It never has and it never will”
items.why: Frequently swapped in, but the original is “It never did and it never will.”
The speech was given on 3 August 1857; the 1857 pamphlet’s title page ↗ prints “Aug. 4th,” and that error is still copied today.

misattribution.truthLine: The authentic line is “Power concedes nothing without a demand. It never did and it never will,” spoken at Canandaigua, N.Y., on 3 August 1857 and printed that year in Two Speeches, by Frederick Douglass ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Douglass delivered the address on the twenty-third anniversary of British emancipation in the West Indies, using the occasion to argue that freedom is won by pressure, not granted by the powerful. The surrounding lines — “If there is no struggle, there is no progress” and “The limits of tyrants are prescribed by the endurance of those whom they oppress” — frame the sentence as a theory of how change actually happens.

Spoken four years before the Civil War, the passage reads as both a diagnosis of slavery’s stubbornness and a call to organized demand. It has since become a staple of civil-rights, labor, and protest rhetoric.
